questions.prompt: After a partition step in quicksort, what is true about the pivot?

options.text: It is in its final sorted position, with smaller elements before and larger after
It is always at the middle index of the array
It is removed from the array
It is duplicated on both sides

questions.explanation: Partitioning places the pivot where it belongs permanently; the two sides are then sorted recursively.

questions.prompt: What are quicksort's average and worst-case time complexities?

options.text: Θ(n log n) average, Θ(n²) worst
Θ(n log n) average, Θ(n log n) worst
Θ(n) average, Θ(n log n) worst

questions.explanation: Balanced partitions give Θ(n log n) on average; maximally unbalanced partitions (extreme pivots) give the Θ(n²) worst case.

questions.prompt: Which statements about quicksort are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: It sorts in place (aside from the recursion stack)
Randomizing the pivot makes the worst case unlikely on any input
A naive last-element pivot is Θ(n²) on already-sorted input

questions.explanation: Quicksort is in-place, randomization defeats worst-case inputs, and a naive pivot is quadratic on sorted data. It is NOT stable.

questions.prompt: The quicksort step that rearranges elements around the pivot is called ______. (one word)
questions.explanation: Partitioning splits the array into elements ≤ pivot and elements > pivot, fixing the pivot's final position.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of a quicksort call on a subarray with more than one element.

items.text: Partition the subarray around the pivot

questions.explanation: Pick a pivot, partition to place it, then recurse on each side; there is no combine step because partitioning already separates the sides.

questions.prompt: Match each concept with its description.

pairs.right: Avoids worst case on any input
Finds the k-th smallest in O(n) average

questions.explanation: These capture quicksort's core: the pivot, the degenerate case, the fix, and the selection variant.
